questions.q: In RS256, which key creates the signature and which key verifies it?
o: Both keys can sign and verify interchangeably
The public key signs, the private key verifies
The private key signs, the public key verifies
A shared derived key does both
questions.x: RS256 is asymmetric RSA. The private key produces the signature and must stay secret on the server. The public key checks the signature and can be shared openly without enabling token forgery.
questions.h: In RSA, the two keys have specific, non-interchangeable roles. Think about which one can be given to everyone and which one must stay secret.

questions.q: Where does the server in this lab publish its RSA public key?
o: /admin
/.env
/jwks.json
/public.pem
questions.x: /jwks.json (JSON Web Key Set) is the standard RFC 7517 endpoint for publishing verification keys. Exposing the public key here is by design and safe for RS256, but becomes a critical input for the algorithm confusion attack.
questions.h: The endpoint is standardized in RFC 7517. Its filename abbreviates three words: JSON Web Key Set.

questions.q: Why is publishing the RSA public key considered safe under normal RS256 usage?
o: The key is encrypted before publishing
Knowing only the public key is mathematically insufficient to produce a valid RS256 signature
The key expires after publication
The public key is a hash, not the real key
questions.x: RSA signatures require the private key to create. The public key only verifies. No matter how many times an attacker downloads the public key, they cannot use it to sign new tokens under RS256.
questions.h: Ask yourself: what operation requires the private key and what operation only requires the public key?

questions.q: What is the root flaw exploited in the algorithm confusion attack?
o: The RSA key pair is too short to resist brute force
The server trusts the alg field in the attacker-controlled JWT header instead of enforcing an expected algorithm from its own config
The JWKS endpoint exposes both keys by mistake
RS256 has a known vulnerability in the SHA-256 hash step
questions.x: A vulnerable server reads the alg claim from the incoming token header and switches its verification logic accordingly. The attacker sets alg to HS256, forcing the server into HMAC mode where the public key becomes the secret.
questions.h: The attacker controls the JWT header. What field in the header can they change to influence which algorithm the server uses for verification?

questions.q: In the attack, what value is used as the HS256 HMAC secret?
o: An empty string from /dev/null
The server's RSA public key material
A randomly generated 256-bit key
The original JWT signature bytes
questions.x: The public key is fetched from /jwks.json and converted to PEM format. The attacker signs with HS256 using that PEM string as the secret. A vulnerable server then verifies the HS256 token using the same public key.
questions.h: If the server verifies an HS256 token using its own public key, what must the attacker use as the HMAC secret when signing?

questions.q: What format does the public key need to be converted into before using it as an HMAC secret?
o: Hex-encoded DER
PEM (Privacy Enhanced Mail) format
Base64url without headers
A JSON string from the JWKS directly
questions.x: JWT libraries that accept an RSA public key as an HS256 secret typically expect it as a PEM-formatted string starting with -----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----. The raw JWKS JSON must be converted to this format first.
questions.h: The standard human-readable format for RSA public keys has a recognizable header line starting with -----BEGIN.

questions.q: After forging the token with algorithm confusion, what payload change grants access to /admin?
o: Changing the alg claim in the payload
Changing sub to administrator
Adding isAdmin: true to the payload
Removing the exp claim
questions.x: The sub (subject) claim identifies the user. Setting it to 'administrator' and signing with HS256 using the public key as the secret produces a token that passes server verification and grants admin access.
questions.h: The algorithm confusion gives you the ability to sign. What payload change do you still need to actually become the admin user?

questions.q: What Python tool was used in the writeup to perform the key conversion and signing?
o: PyCryptodome only
hashcat with mode 16500
PyJWT combined with the cryptography library
OpenSSL command line
questions.x: PyJWT handles JWT creation and signing. The cryptography library converts the JWKS JSON to a PEM-formatted public key object. Together they produce an HS256-signed token using the public key as the secret.
questions.h: Two Python packages are combined in the writeup: one for JWT handling and one for cryptographic key operations.

questions.q: What server-side configuration change would fully prevent algorithm confusion attacks?
o: Rotate the RSA key pair more frequently
Enforce the expected algorithm from server configuration and reject tokens claiming any other algorithm
Restrict the JWKS endpoint to authenticated users
Use 4096-bit RSA instead of 2048-bit
questions.x: The server must decide which algorithm it accepts based on its own deployment configuration, not the token header. If it expects RS256, any token claiming HS256 should be rejected before verification even begins.
questions.h: The flaw is that the server listens to the attacker's alg value. What is the opposite of that behavior?

questions.q: If the server correctly enforced RS256 only, what would happen when the forged HS256 token arrives?
o: The server would try both algorithms and use whichever passes
The token would be rejected because the algorithm does not match the expected RS256
The server would log the attempt but still process the token
The public key would be regenerated automatically
questions.x: A hardened server compares the alg claim against its expected value first. HS256 does not match RS256, so the token is rejected immediately. No key material is consulted and no payload is read.
questions.h: If the server has already decided it only accepts RS256, what does it do when it sees a different algorithm in the header?
